Catches leaving the motive as a `Hole` in a `Match`. `fill_match_motives` (elaborate.rs:578-636) fills a `Hole` motive only from an EXPECTED type; with none available and a λ-shaped first case it errors with "cannot infer the motive of this `match`" (elaborate.rs:660-665). Emitting motives explicitly sidesteps this entirely — see T04-011.
oracle: The emitted term contains no `Term::Hole` and no `?`-prefixed `Term::Var`; every motive appears as an explicit `Term::Lambda`; `infer_type` succeeds; and the emitted motive is term-for-term the translation of the motive in Lean's `Expr`, not one re-derived by LOGOS's unifier.

cases.title: Elaboration postponement order — LOGOS's elaborator has fixed phases, not a queue
cases.lean: postponed elaboration of lambdas/literals against unknown expected types, `default_instance` resolution after postponement, `(· + 1)` sections, numeric-literal defaulting to `Nat`
cases.target: The term Lean's elaborator ultimately produced, with every postponed decision already made — including the DEFAULT instance Lean picked when nothing constrained a numeric literal's type. Plus a loss record naming each decision that LOGOS's own elaborator would make differently.
evidence: kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1029-1045 (`elaborate_app`: implicit positions get a fresh metavariable immediately; INSTANCE positions are DEFERRED — "only AFTER the explicit arguments have been processed" — this two-phase order is the whole of LOGOS's postponement machinery); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1046-1080 (`elaborate_app_against`: the expected-type pass runs BEFORE instance resolution, a third fixed phase — there is no queue, no re-scheduling, and no "try again when more is known" loop); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:216-292 (`unify_in` is a single pass: a constraint that cannot be solved now is a FAILURE, not a postponement — there is no constraint store); kernel/src/context.rs:184-188 (`add_instance` is a flat `Vec`, first-match-wins: there is no `default_instance` notion at all); kernel/src/term.rs:538 (`Term::Lit` — a literal's type is decided by `infer_type` (type_checker.rs:294-311) from the literal's KIND, not from context: `Literal::Nat` is always `Nat`, `Literal::Int` always `Int`)
guards: **Translate the post-elaboration `Expr`, never the surface `Syntax`.** This case is the reason the rule is stated as *post*-elaboration and not merely "after parsing". `fun x => x + 1` has no type in `Syntax`; it acquires one only after Lean's queue drains and defaulting fires. A translator on `Syntax` must reimplement the queue, the re-scheduling, and the defaulting table — three mechanisms LOGOS does not have and Lean does not document as stable.

Catches translating a numeric literal without its resolved type. `Term::Lit`'s type is read off the literal's KIND (type_checker.rs:294-311): `Literal::Nat` is `Nat` and `Literal::Int` is `Int`, and LOGOS's `Nat` (inductive) and `Int` (opaque, with axiomatised ring laws) are completely different things (LOGOS_FACTS). A translator that emits `Literal::Nat` for a Lean literal Lean elaborated at `Int` has changed the type AND lost every computation rule — see T10-004.

Catches the instance-phase order. LOGOS resolves instances only after the explicit arguments and the expected type (elaborate.rs:1029-1080). A translator that re-resolves instances itself, earlier, may pick a different one from the flat first-match list — and since both have the class type, the emitted term typechecks and computes differently.

Catches assuming a failed constraint will be retried. `unify_in` (elaborate.rs:216-292) has no constraint store: a constraint that cannot be solved at the moment it is raised is a hard failure. A translator that emits terms in a different ORDER than Lean elaborated them (say, all types before all values) can therefore raise a constraint before its solution is known and fail on a term Lean accepted.

Catches `(· + 1)` sections and other syntax whose elaboration is postponed twice — once for the section's own lambda and once for the `HAdd` instance. The emitted term must be the fully-resolved `fun x : Nat => Nat.add x 1`-shaped term, not a polymorphic skeleton.

Catches a postponed decision that Lean made from a LATER line. In `laterPin` below nothing in the definition constrains the literal; the ascription on the following `example` is what pins it in the source's reading order but not in the elaborator's.
oracle: Every numeric literal in the emitted term carries the type Lean gave it (`Nat` vs `Int` vs a user `OfNat`), checkable by `infer_type` on the emitted `Lit`; every instance argument is the one in Lean's `Expr`; the emitted term contains no `Hole` and no `?`-prefixed `Var`; and the loss record contains POSTPONEMENT_ORDER listing each defaulted decision.
loss: POSTPONEMENT_ORDER. Lean's elaborator maintains a queue of postponed problems and re-runs them as metavariables get solved, then applies `default_instance`s to whatever is still unresolved. LOGOS has three fixed phases and no queue. Any decision Lean made by postponement — most importantly, which `OfNat` instance a bare numeric literal got — has to be baked into the emitted term. The loss record must name each such decision, because a later re-elaboration on the LOGOS side will not reproduce it.

DEFAULT_INSTANCE_ABSENCE. Lean's `@[default_instance]` is what makes `fun x => x + 1` elaborate at `Nat` rather than staying polymorphic. LOGOS has no default-instance mechanism (context.rs:184-188 is the whole instance system), so the defaulted type is not recoverable from the LOGOS side and must be recorded. See T07-007.

cases.title: `..` ellipsis — sugar for "fill the rest with `_`", expanded before translation
cases.lean: `{ x := 1, .. }` structure-instance ellipsis, `| .mk .. =>` and `| { x := v, .. } =>` pattern ellipsis, `f ..` trailing application ellipsis
cases.target: The fully-expanded, fully-SOLVED form. `..` is Lean's sugar for supplying `_` in every remaining position, so the emitted term is whatever those holes were solved to: a full-arity constructor application, a case λ-abstracting every field, or a full application spine. The emitted term must contain **no `Term::Hole`**.
evidence: kernel/src/context.rs:271-369 (`add_structure` generates ONE `{name}_mk` constructor of full field arity — there is no partial-constructor form); kernel/src/type_checker.rs:255-259 (`cases.len()` must equal the constructor count) and :778-830 (`compute_case_type`: a case's expected type is the constructor's REMAINING Π-telescope, so a case must bind every field); kernel/src/term.rs:487-492 (`Term::Match` has no pattern language at all, hence no ellipsis) and :478 (`App` is positional and binary); kernel/src/term.rs:540-544 and kernel/src/type_checker.rs:313 (`Term::Hole` is the only "unknown" and it is `CannotInferHole` at `infer_type`) and :1593-1597 (`types_equal` treats `Hole` as matching **anything**); kernel/src/termination.rs:403-415 (`count_pi_params` / `extract_lambda_params`: the guard peels exactly as many λs from a case as the constructor has Π binders)
guards: **Translate the post-elaboration `Expr`, never the surface `Syntax`.** All three ellipses are pure surface: Lean expands each to `_`s and then solves them. The `Expr` has no trace of them. A translator on `Syntax` must reimplement the expansion AND the unification that fills it — and since the fill is by unification, not by defaults, the answer depends on the whole surrounding elaboration problem.

Catches emitting `Term::Hole` for an ellipsis-supplied position. `types_equal` matches a `Hole` against **anything** (type_checker.rs:1593-1597) and the leniency leaks into `is_subtype`'s fast path (:1314), so an ellipsis that the translator did not resolve produces a declaration that typechecks against any type. Since `..` is exactly "I did not write this out", it is the most likely place for a translator to leave one.

Catches emitting a SHORT constructor application for a structure-instance ellipsis. `add_structure`'s `{name}_mk` takes every field (context.rs:271-369), so a two-argument spine against a three-field constructor is a partial application of type `Nat → Three`, not a `Three`. Where the omitted field's type makes that partial application well-typed in context, it typechecks and yields a function where a value was meant.

Catches emitting an under-bound CASE for `| .mk .. =>`. The case must λ-abstract every field. `compute_case_type` (type_checker.rs:778-830) catches the arity slip when the body's type differs — but `termination.rs:410-415` peels `count_pi_params` λs regardless, so under a `Fix` an under-bound case makes the guard peel into the case BODY and mark a non-field variable as structurally smaller. That admits a non-terminating fixpoint: a soundness hole, not a type error.

Catches `..` inside a NESTED pattern, where the ellipsis belongs to the inner constructor. Each nesting level of the emitted match tree needs its own full binder list (see T04-008), and an ellipsis at the outer level says nothing about the inner.

Catches confusing `..` with structure UPDATE (`{ s with x := 1 }`). Update reads the remaining fields off `s` via its projections, so the emitted term mentions `s` three times; `..` does not mention any receiver at all. Emitting one for the other changes which term the fields come from.

Catches a trailing-only parse assumption. `..` is legal only in trailing position (`@idf .. 5` is a parse error), so a translator that normalises an `Expr` back to surface text cannot re-introduce `..` wherever a `_` appears.
oracle: The emitted term contains no `Term::Hole`; the emitted constructor application has the structure's full field arity; every emitted match case λ-abstracts exactly `count_pi_params(ctor_type)` binders; `infer_type` succeeds; and the emitted term is term-for-term identical to the translation of the same expression written without any `..`.
note: INDEX.md lists this case as `translate`, which is right, but the reason is narrower than "`..` fills in defaults". In Lean 4.14 `..` does **not** apply a field's `:=` default — it substitutes `_`, and the elaboration then succeeds only if unification solves it. `{ val := 1, .. }` on a structure whose `tag` merely has a default is an ERROR ("don't know how to synthesize placeholder"), whereas `{ val := 1 }` succeeds by defaulting. Default-value inlining is therefore T05-006, not this case; `..` belongs with the holes of T05-013.

cases.title: `OfNat` literal elaboration — LOGOS literals are typed by KIND, not by instance
cases.lean: OfNat, numeric literals at a user type, `@[default_instance] instOfNatNat`, `(5 : Int)` vs `(5 : Nat)` vs `(5 : MyNum)`
cases.target: For a literal Lean elaborated at `Nat`: `Term::Lit(Literal::Nat(BigInt))`. For one at `Int`: `Term::Lit(Literal::Int(i64))` / `Literal::BigInt`. For one at a USER type: the fully-applied `OfNat.ofNat` term from Lean's `Expr`, i.e. the instance's projection applied to the raw literal — never a bare `Term::Lit`, because LOGOS has no way to give a literal a user type.

A translator on `Syntax` must reimplement `OfNat` resolution AND Lean's defaulting table to recover which; a translator on `Expr` reads the instance off the application.

Catches emitting `Literal::Nat` for a literal Lean elaborated at `Int`. The emitted term then has type `Nat` (type_checker.rs:294-311), which is an INDUCTIVE with a `Zero`/`Succ` computation rule, where the source meant `Int`, which is OPAQUE with only axiomatised ring laws. Every `rfl` the source proved by computation stops holding, and — because LOGOS is cumulative and both are `Type 0` — many surrounding terms still typecheck. This is T10-004 reached through the elaborator.

Catches emitting a bare `Literal::Nat` for a literal at a USER type. There is no `Literal` variant for it, so the emitted term has type `Nat` where the source had `MyNum`. If `MyNum` is a one-field wrapper around `Nat`, `try_structure_eta` (type_checker.rs:1391-1417) may make the two definitionally equal inside `def_eq` — so the mistranslation typechecks in exactly the case where it is most tempting.

Catches emitting a NEGATIVE `Literal::Nat`. `infer_type` rejects it explicitly (type_checker.rs:298-303: "a `Nat` literal must be non-negative"), and `extract_constructor` (reduction.rs:336-345) collapses a negative literal to `Zero` so the Peano peel terminates — so a negative `Nat` literal that slips past a different code path computes as `0` rather than failing.

Catches losing the `BigInt` boundary. `Literal::Int(i64)` and `Literal::BigInt` are different variants (term.rs:13-44) that both infer to `Global("Int")`; a translator that canonicalises them inconsistently produces two terms that are equal in meaning but not syntactically, and LOGOS's `types_equal`/`unify` compare literals by equality (elaborate.rs:275) — so they will fail to unify. See T10-002.

A translator on `Syntax` that "erases ascriptions and translates the rest" therefore translates a different program. A translator on `Expr` sees only the result, which is exactly right.

Catches emitting an ascription as an identity application. Lean's `(e : T)` for a `Type`-valued `T` elaborates to just `e`; a translator that emits `App(Global("id"), e)` adds a delta step that counts against `normalize`'s 10000 fuel (reduction.rs:52-69) and, more importantly, changes the term's SHAPE — so any later pattern-match on the emitted term (a proof script, a `simp` set) no longer fires.

Catches emitting `show T from e` as anything other than `e`. In Lean `show T from e` is `(e : T)` and `show T by tac` is a tactic block; the first leaves no trace, the second leaves the tactic's proof term. A translator that treats them uniformly either loses a proof or invents one.

Catches the interaction with LOGOS's CUMULATIVITY. `is_subtype_normalized` admits `Prop ≤ Type 0 ≤ Type 1` (type_checker.rs:1330-1360) where Lean admits none. An ascription that Lean used to force a *specific* universe — `(α : Type 1)` on something that would otherwise be `Type 0` — is erased, and the LOGOS term then typechecks at the smaller universe too. The ascription's constraint is simply gone, so a translator that relies on "it still typechecks" to validate its output has no signal here. See T01-009 and T11-001.

Catches an ascription that drives COERCION insertion. `(b : Nat)` with `b : Bool` inserts `boolToNat b` (T05-011); the emitted term must contain that application. A translator that strips the ascription and emits the bare `b` produces a `Bool` where a `Nat` was meant.

Catches an ascription inside a `match` branch, which is how Lean is often told the motive. Erasing it is harmless in Lean (the motive is already in the `Expr`) but a `Syntax`-level translator that erases it then has to infer the motive itself, and LOGOS's `infer_match_motive` is Miller-restricted (T04-011).

cases.target: (none — no sound translation)

An `Expr`-level translator sees the RESULT of that transformation — and the result is a tower of applications of `Bind.bind`, `Pure.pure`, `ForIn.forIn` and the monad's instance projections, none of which exist in LOGOS. So reading `Expr` turns an impossible re-implementation into a clean, precise rejection, which is the whole value.

An emitted `SProp` proposition has no constructors to prove it with.

Catches the specific partiality trap exercised by `irrelevanceUnderBinder` below: a proof whose type mentions a variable bound in an enclosing `Pi` is only typeable in the EXTENDED context, and `proof_irrelevant` calls `infer_type(ctx, …)` against the context it was handed. If the translator hoists a proof term out of its binder (a tempting CSE optimisation under the named representation), `infer_type` returns `Err(UnboundVariable)` and irrelevance silently reports "not equal" instead of reporting an error.
oracle: Each `rfl` below that Lean accepts by irrelevance must be checked against LOGOS `def_eq`; every one that LOGOS's `proof_irrelevant` declines must appear in the loss record under PROOF_IRRELEVANCE_PARTIALITY. Silent success with no loss record is a failure of this case.
loss: PROOF_IRRELEVANCE_PARTIALITY. Lean's proof irrelevance is a TOTAL definitional rule applied by the kernel's `whnf`/`isDefEq` on any two terms whose type is a `Prop` — it never fails for well-typed input. LOGOS's is a *fallible predicate*: it returns `false` (meaning "not equal") whenever `infer_type` errors on either side, whenever `infer_type` of the type does not NORMALIZE to `Sort(Prop)` within the 10000-step fuel, or whenever the two propositions are not `def_eq`. So a Lean proof that is accepted by irrelevance can be REJECTED by LOGOS. The loss is one-directional — LOGOS never accepts more here than Lean does — so it is a degrade, not a soundness reject; but a translator that assumes it is total will produce certificates that fail to check for reasons the diagnostic will not explain.

COST. `proof_irrelevant` runs up to four `infer_type` calls per comparison, and `infer_type` itself calls `normalize`. Because the rule sits at the BOTTOM of `def_eq_normalized`, every FAILING definitional-equality check in the whole development pays this cost before reporting failure. A translator that emits many small propositional obligations turns an O(n) check into an O(n · |term|) one.

P → Q → And P Q`); kernel/src/prelude.rs:1847-1909 (`register_or`, constructors named `left` and `right` — NOT `inl`/`inr`); kernel/src/prelude.rs:722-727 (`True` + constructor `I`); kernel/src/prelude.rs:729-733 (`False`, zero constructors); kernel/src/prelude.rs:735-755 (`Not` is an `add_definition`, body `λ(P:Prop). Π(_:P). False` — a DEFINITION, so delta-transparent, not an inductive); a grep of `crates/logicaffeine_kernel/src` for `Iff` returns NOTHING — there is no biconditional anywhere in the kernel or prelude
guards: Catches emitting `Or.inl`/`Or.inr` verbatim. LOGOS's constructors are literally named `left` and `right` (prelude.rs:1847-1909) and lookup is by flat `String` (context.rs:449), so `Global("Or.inl")` resolves to nothing and `Global("inl")` resolves to nothing. Worse, `left` and `right` are ALSO the names of two tactic script primitives, so a translator that "helpfully" registers its own `inl` ends up with two constructor names for one inductive and `Match`'s positional case list (type_checker.rs:254-260) no longer lines up with registration order.

Catches treating `Not` as opaque. LOGOS's `Not` is an `add_definition` (prelude.rs:755), hence delta-transparent: `Not P` and `P → False` are definitionally equal and a proof of one is a proof of the other with NO coercion. A translator that emits `Not` as an `add_declaration` (axiom) makes `¬p` an opaque `Prop` with no inhabitants and no elimination rule — every `absurd`/`Not.elim` downstream becomes unprovable. Symmetrically, a translator that ALWAYS inlines `P → False` loses the head symbol that the instance-resolution `class_heads` scan and the `cases` tactic key on.

Catches assuming `Iff` exists. It does not. `p ↔ q` must be emitted as a new definition; emitting it as an `add_declaration` axiom would make the biconditional opaque (no `.mp`/`.mpr`), and emitting it as an `add_inductive` with an `Iff_intro` constructor would give a DIFFERENT proposition from `And (P→Q) (Q→P)` — one that `propext`-style reasoning cannot bridge, since `propext` is absent too (T06-010).

`And` is registered with `add_inductive` (prelude.rs:1816), which treats the FULL arity as parameters (context.rs:253). Both `P` and `Q` are therefore parameters and `derive_recursor` builds a zero-index eliminator. A translator re-registering `And` via `add_indexed_inductive` with a different `num_params` silently changes the recursor's telescope.

`Or` has TWO constructors, so `is_subsingleton_prop` is false (type_checker.rs:1716) and `derive_recursor` pins its motive to `Sort(Prop)` (recursor.rs:64-71): `Or` cannot be large-eliminated into `Type`. `And` and `False` CAN. Lean agrees on `Or` and `False`; a translator must not assume a uniform rule. See T06-015 and T01-014.
oracle: Every emitted connective term typechecks; `Or` constructors are emitted as `left`/ `right`; `Not` is referenced as the prelude DEFINITION; `Iff` is emitted exactly once via `add_definition` and never via `add_declaration` or `add_inductive`.

cases.title: Universal quantification — `∀` is `Term::Pi`, and its result sort comes from `imax`

cases.target:
`∀ (x : α), P x` ⟼ `Term::Pi { param: "x", param_type: <α>, body_type:

}`. There is no separate `Forall` constant: universal quantification over a proposition IS the dependent function type, exactly as in Lean. The result sort is computed by `Universe::imax(sort α, sort (P x))`, which collapses to `Prop` whenever the body is a `Prop` — so quantification over ANY domain, including `Type 1`, still yields a `Prop`. That is impredicativity and LOGOS has it.
evidence: kernel/src/term.rs:463 (`Term::Pi { param, param_type, body_type }`); kernel/src/type_checker.rs:108 (Pi formation computes the result sort with `imax`, matching Lean); kernel/src/term.rs:167-191 (`Universe::IMax` is a first-class universe former); kernel/src/prelude.rs:53-78 (`dne`'s own type is a `Pi` whose `param_type` is `Sort(Universe::Prop)` — the prelude itself relies on impredicative quantification over `Prop`)

LOGOS's `Display` renders a `Pi` whose `param == "_"` as a non-dependent arrow (term.rs:585-590), so the mistake is invisible in printed output while the body still contains `Var("_")`, which the next `"_"`-named binder will capture. Lean's binder names are hints carried alongside de Bruijn indices, so the translator must decide from OCCURRENCE, not from the name.

Catches emitting a `Lambda` where a `Pi` is meant. Both variants have the same three fields with nearly the same names (`body` vs `body_type`, term.rs:463-470), and a `∀` whose body is a `Prop` and a `fun` whose body is a proof are easy to transpose in a generic lowering. A `Lambda` in type position infers a `Pi` type, so `infer_type` succeeds and the error only surfaces much later as an unexplainable mismatch.

Catches *hard-coding* the result sort instead of using `imax`. `∀ α : Type, P α` is a `Prop` in Lean and must be one in LOGOS. A translator that computes the result universe as `max` rather than `imax` puts `bigDomainProp` below in `Type 1`, at which point the proposition is no longer a `Prop` and proof irrelevance (type_checker.rs:1547-1567) stops applying to its proofs — silently, because LOGOS is cumulative (type_checker.rs:1330-1360) and a `Type 1` "proposition" still typechecks everywhere a `Prop` was expected downstream of a `Sort`-valued binder.

Catches the shadowing trap in `shadowed` below. Two nested `∀` binders may share a name in Lean (they are de Bruijn); in LOGOS's NAMED representation the inner one shadows the outer, and `substitute_avoiding` (type_checker.rs:1088) alpha-renames only when a replacement's free variables collide. Nested same-name binders must be freshened at emit time.
oracle: `infer_type` on each emitted `Pi` returns a `Sort`, and for every declaration whose Lean type is a `Prop` the inferred `Sort` normalizes to `Sort(Universe::Prop)`; no emitted dependent `Pi` has `param == "_"`.

((P → False) → False) → P` with literal `Pi` binders named `"_"` (prelude.rs:56-77) — it does NOT mention the `Not` global. The proof terms that use it typecheck in the translator's own `Context`. Nothing warns. And the trusted base has just grown by an axiom that is strictly stronger than everything LOGOS deliberately chose to trust — `choice` gives `propDecidable`, hence full `Decidable` for every `Prop`, hence `decide`-based "computation" on undecidable propositions; combined with the `Quot` primitives already in the prelude (prelude.rs:1230-1338) it gives Diaconescu's theorem, i.e. excluded middle *again* but now with data. The `dne` axiom alone gives none of that.

The failure is SILENT IN THE PLACE THAT MATTERS. `certificate::recheck` rebuilds the context from `StandardLibrary::register` alone (certificate.rs:73-75), so a certificate whose proof term mentions the invented axiom fails with a bare `KernelError::UnboundVariable("Classical_choice")` — a message that looks like a name resolution bug, not like "you added an axiom". The de Bruijn criterion is broken and the artefact that was supposed to record the breakage says everything is fine.

Catches the "it's just `Nonempty` elimination" rationalisation. `Nonempty α` is a `Prop` and `α` is data; eliminating the former into the latter is EXACTLY the content of choice. LOGOS has no `Nonempty` at all, and its `Prop`-elimination gate (`is_subsingleton_prop`, type_checker.rs:1688-1716) permits large elimination only for zero-constructor or single-propositional-field inductives — a translator that declares `Nonempty` as such an inductive and then large-eliminates it has written choice by hand.

Catches the scale error. This is not one missing lemma. `Classical.choice` is one of Lean 4's three core axioms and essentially the whole of Mathlib depends on it transitively; `#print axioms` on almost any Mathlib theorem lists it. A translator that rejects it correctly will reject most real Lean input — which is the honest answer, and is what this corpus exists to establish.

The `Lambda`/`Lambda` arm of `def_eq_normalized` (type_checker.rs:1530-1535) renames one binder and recurses on the BODIES — so it proves `(λx. e₁) ≡ (λx. e₂)` exactly when `e₁ ≡ e₂` as open terms under `normalize` (fuel 10000, reduction.rs:52-69). That is intensional. `funext` is needed precisely when the bodies are equal only because of a HYPOTHESIS (`h : ∀ x, f x = g x`), which `normalize` cannot use. `pointwiseNotDefEq` below is the discriminating instance: `Nat.add n 0` and `n` are propositionally but not definitionally equal in Lean, so the two functions are NOT `def_eq` in LOGOS and `funext` is genuinely required.

cases.title: `native_decide` — LOGOS has the same two axioms, but a DIFFERENT evaluator in the TCB

They are not interchangeable: `decide` reduces by ordinary kernel normalization under the 10000-step fuel (reduction.rs:52-69) and is in NO ONE'S trusted base, whereas `reduceBool` short- circuits to the evaluator. Downgrading `native_decide` to `decide` will usually fail (fuel exhaustion returns a PARTIALLY reduced term, silently — reduction.rs:57-60 — so the `rfl` does not close and the failure looks like a mysterious type mismatch), and upgrading `decide` to `native_decide` silently enlarges the TCB.

Catches emitting `reduceBool` as a DEFINITION with body `λb. b`. Its doc comment says it "is the identity" (prelude.rs:1190), which invites exactly this. But making it a definition destroys the mechanism: `try_reflection_reduce`/the `reduceBool` arm in `reduce_step` matches on `Term::Global("reduceBool")` applied to an argument (reduction.rs:111-115), and a delta-transparent definition would be unfolded to the identity BEFORE that arm is reached, so the evaluator never runs and the `rfl` fails.

Catches emitting a `Term::Hole` for the `b` argument of `ofReduceBool`. Because `types_equal` matches `Hole` against anything (type_checker.rs:1594-1597), a `native_decide` certificate with a hole in the result position would be accepted for ANY `Bool` — turning a trusted-evaluator appeal into an unconditional one.
oracle: Emitted terms typecheck and reduce; both globals are emitted via `add_declaration` with the prelude's exact spellings; every declaration whose proof term mentions them carries a loss record naming EVALUATOR_IDENTITY; and no `Term::Hole` appears in the emitted `ofReduceBool` application.
loss: EVALUATOR_IDENTITY. Lean's `native_decide` trusts the Lean compiler, its C code generator, the resulting native object code, and the `Decidable` instance's compiled form. LOGOS's trusts `crate::eval::eval_bool`, a CBV interpreter inside the kernel (reduction.rs:109-115). The two axioms have the same TYPES, so the translation is type-correct and the certificate re-checks — but the proposition "this `Bool` computation evaluates to `true`" is now being asserted by a DIFFERENT program. A `native_decide` proof that is sound in Lean is not thereby sound in LOGOS, and vice versa. The loss record must name both evaluators so a reviewer can see what changed.

TCB_EXPANSION_IS_INHERITED. `reduceBool`/`ofReduceBool` are genuine `add_declaration` axioms (prelude.rs:1206,1208) — unlike `decide`, `of_decide_eq_true`, `Eq_rec_dep`, `Eq_sym` and `Eq_trans`, which the prelude deliberately PROVES. Every theorem whose proof term mentions them has a strictly larger trusted base than one that does not, and nothing in the certificate distinguishes them: `PRELUDE_VERSION` is a single constant string (certificate.rs:28) covering the whole prelude. The translator must therefore emit a per-declaration loss record; a corpus-level `#print axioms` equivalent cannot be recovered afterwards.
note: INDEX.md marks this `degrade`, which this file follows. A translator whose policy is "never expand the trusted base" (the T06-009/010/011 stance) may legitimately escalate this to `reject` instead — the two axioms ARE in the LOGOS prelude, so it is not a base expansion, but the evaluator behind them is not the one the Lean proof appealed to. Either verdict is defensible; a SILENT translation is not.

See T00-016 and T11-004.

The translator must propagate the taint through the dependency graph of ELABORATED terms, exactly as Lean's `#print axioms` does, and reject every declaration in the closure — not just the one with the keyword in its source.

Catches the "translate it as an `add_declaration` and record a loss" compromise. There is no acceptable loss record for this: a loss record documents information that could not be carried, whereas this documents a proposition that was never proved. `reject` is the only correct verdict, which is why INDEX.md marks it `R` and why this case has no `@loss` field.
oracle: Translator exits non-zero with E_INCOMPLETE_PROOF for EVERY declaration in this file — including `taintedUser`, which contains no `sorry` — and performs zero `add_declaration`, `add_definition` and `add_instance` calls. A harness additionally asserts that no emitted term anywhere in the corpus contains `Term::Hole`.
diag: E_INCOMPLETE_PROOF — must name the declaration, name `sorryAx`, and state that no output was produced. It must be a hard error, not a warning, and it must be non-suppressible. A translator that offers a `--allow-sorry` flag has built the bug.
note: This file deliberately emits Lean's `declaration uses 'sorry'` WARNING — on exactly THREE declarations: `taintedLemma`, `tacticSorry` and `dataSorry`. `lean` still exits 0, so a harness keyed on the exit code sees a clean build. That is the first half of the lesson. The second half is that `taintedUser` gets NO warning at all: its proof term mentions the constant `taintedLemma`, not `sorryAx`, so the warning does not propagate. A translator that treats the warning as its taint signal will therefore translate `taintedUser` and emit a "verified" LOGOS theorem resting on an unproved lemma. The taint must be computed over the transitive closure of the elaborated environment — what `#print axioms` reports — not over warnings and not over source text.

cases.title: Classical content that goes BEYOND `dne` — `Classical.byCases` is fine, its `Decidable`-producing relatives are not
cases.lean: Classical.byCases, Classical.not_forall, Classical.skolem, Classical.axiomOfChoice, Classical.decEq, Classical.dec, `open Classical in` instance activation
cases.target: (none — for the declarations below that need choice. The PROP-only fragment (`Classical.byCases`, `not_forall` at a decidable-free statement) is derivable from `dne` and belongs to T06-008; everything in this file is deliberately outside it.)

It is not. The step from `p ∨ ¬p` to `Decidable p` crosses the `Prop`/`Type` boundary, and LOGOS blocks it structurally: `Or` has two constructors, so `is_subsingleton_prop` is false (type_checker.rs:1688-1716) and the derived eliminator's motive is pinned to `Sort(Prop)` (recursor.rs:64-71). Catches the blanket-instance disaster. `open Classical in` activates `Classical.propDecidable` as a low-priority instance in Lean, and it then silently discharges every `Decidable` goal in scope. Translated naively that becomes ONE `add_instance` entry in LOGOS's flat `Vec<(Term,Term)>` (context.rs:184). LOGOS has no priorities: `resolve_instance_at` scans the vector in INSERTION ORDER and the first that unifies wins (elaborate.rs:1331-1340). So the blanket instance either shadows `decEqNat`/`decEqBool` entirely (if inserted first) or is dead (if inserted last), and which one happens depends on translation order. See T07-007 and T07-008.

Catches `Classical.skolem` / `axiomOfChoice`. These are choice with a function produced, not merely a witness; translating them requires `Classical.choice` (T06-009) AND `funext` (T06-011) to state the extensionality of the chosen function. Rejecting one of the three and emitting the others is the worst outcome: the emitted fragment typechecks, so the rejection looks like a localised gap rather than a structural one.

Catches `Classical.not_forall`. Its statement `(¬∀ x, p x) ↔ ∃ x, ¬p x` is pure `Prop` and IS derivable from `dne` — but its Lean proof goes through `Classical.byContradiction` plus `Classical.em` at the INSTANTIATED predicate, and the elaborated term in Lean 4 core mentions `Classical.choice` through `Classical.propDecidable`. A translator that re-derives the statement from `dne` is correct and must say so in its output; a translator that translates Lean's PROOF TERM verbatim will drag choice in. cases.title: `class` declaration — LOGOS has no class concept; a class is a structure plus entries in a flat instance list
cases.lean: class, class methods, instance-implicit binders `[C α]`, `#print` of a class's structure representation
cases.target: Three separate LOGOS actions, none of which is "declare a class": 1. `Context::add_structure(name, params, fields)` — the carrier. This yields the inductive, the constructor `{name}_mk`, one DEFINITION per field whose body is a `Term::Match`, and the `StructInfo` that gates eta. The sort is hard-coded `Type 0`. 2. `Context::set_binder_kinds(user, kinds)` with `ParamKind::Instance` at each `[C α]` position, so the elaborator knows to resolve rather than unify there. 3. `Context::add_instance(ty, value)` per instance — see T07-002. A class with NO instances is not a class at all in LOGOS: `class_heads` is computed from the registered INSTANCES, so a head with no instance is never recognised as an instance premise.
evidence: kernel/src/context.rs:271-369 (`add_structure` — the only record-declaring API); kernel/src/context.rs:300 (`let ind_type = pis(params, Term::Sort(Universe::Type(0)))` — the sort is hard-coded); kernel/src/context.rs:71 (`instances: Arc<Vec<(Term, Term)>>` — the ENTIRE class system is one flat vector of pairs); kernel/src/context.rs:184-186 (`add_instance` pushes onto it; there is no key, no priority, no class name, no coherence check); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1016-1027 (`ParamKind::{Explicit, Implicit, Instance}` — the only place "instance" appears as a concept, and it is a per-BINDER annotation, not a declaration form); kernel/src/context.rs:201-207 (`set_binder_kinds`); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1174-1189 (`class_heads` — the set of "typeclass heads" is derived by scanning every registered INSTANCE's conclusion for its head `Global`); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1321-1341 (`resolve_instance_at` — a linear scan of `ctx.instances()` in insertion order, first success wins, depth-bounded by `MAX_INSTANCE_DEPTH = 64` at :1160)
guards: Catches emitting a class as an `add_inductive` + hand-written projections. The projections MUST come from `add_structure`, because only `add_structure` registers the `StructInfo` that `try_structure_eta` consults (type_checker.rs:1391-1417, gated at :1473-1478). Without it, eta silently stops firing for that class and `⟨c.f, c.g⟩ ≡ c` becomes unprovable — which breaks every `extends`-flattening argument in T07-005.

Catches forgetting `set_binder_kinds`. A `[C α]` binder translated as an ordinary `Pi` is an EXPLICIT parameter in LOGOS: `elab_surface`'s application path (elaborate.rs:948-962) falls back to `implicit_args` leading-implicits when the recorded kinds do not match the argument count, so every call site must then pass the dictionary by hand. Worse, the fallback at :958-962 will happily accept a DIFFERENT arity than intended and silently reinterpret which arguments are implicit.

Catches assuming method names survive. `add_structure` emits projections named `format!("{name}_{field}")` (context.rs:310-362, looked up by `elaborate_dot` at elaborate.rs:1284), so `Semigroup.op` becomes the flat `String` `"Semigroup_op"`. Lean's `Semigroup.op` and a user's `def Semigroup_op` collide — see T02-020.
oracle: For each class below: exactly one `add_structure` call with the class's name; one `set_binder_kinds` call per consumer carrying `ParamKind::Instance` at the right positions; and a loss record naming NO_CLASS_IDENTITY. `PropClass` and `BigClass` must be escalated (E_STRUCTURE_SORT_NOT_TYPE0). A class declared with no instance must additionally carry EMPTY_CLASS_IS_INVISIBLE.
loss: NO_CLASS_IDENTITY. Lean's `class C` creates a distinguished environment entry with an attribute, an instance table keyed on it, priorities, an `outParam` mask, default instances, and a `Std.TagAttribute` that `#print axioms`-style tooling can query. LOGOS has none of that. After translation, a class is indistinguishable from any other structure, and its instance-hood is inferred *a posteriori* from the shape of whatever was pushed into `instances`. Nothing can be reported back: there is no way to ask "what are the instances of `C`", only "what unifies with this goal".

EMPTY_CLASS_IS_INVISIBLE. Because `class_heads` (elaborate.rs:1178-1189) is built by folding over `ctx.instances()`, a class with zero registered instances contributes no head. A `[C α]` binder for such a class is therefore NOT treated as an instance premise during resolution — `try_instance` (elaborate.rs:1346-1400) classifies a parameter as a premise only when its head is in `class_heads`. So a class declared before any of its instances, or a class whose instances all failed to translate, degrades into an ordinary implicit argument that unification must solve. It usually cannot, and the error is `no typeclass instance found` (elaborate.rs:1147-1152) or a stuck metavariable — never "this class has no instances".

SORT_PINNING. `add_structure` hard-codes `Type 0` (context.rs:300). A Lean `class` in `Prop` (a *mixin* like `Std.Associative`) or in `Type u` for `u ≥ 1` cannot be declared this way at all. `PropClass` and `BigClass` below are the instances; this is the same wall as T03-012 and it is what makes T07-011 a rejection.

cases.title: `instance` declaration — one `add_definition` plus one `add_instance` entry
cases.lean: instance, named instance, `instance : C α := ⟨…⟩`, anonymous instance naming
cases.target: Two calls per instance, in this order: 1. `Context::add_definition(name, <class type>, <dictionary value>)` — the instance's VALUE, an application of the structure constructor `{Class}_mk`. 2. `Context::add_instance(<class type>, Global(name))` — the search entry. Note the second argument is the instance's *value term*; pushing the unfolded body here rather than the `Global` makes the resolved instance delta-transparent at every use site and defeats the elaborator's deliberate choice to "[b]ind directly (not via normalizing unification) so the instance stays structured rather than being δ-unfolded into its body".
evidence: kernel/src/context.rs:180-186 (`add_instance(ty, value)`: "Register a typeclass instance: a `value` of type `ty` (e.g. `mk Nat Zero` of type `Inhabited Nat`). The elaborator resolves an instance-implicit argument by searching these for a `ty` that unifies with the required class type"); kernel/src/context.rs:71 (the backing store is `Arc<Vec<(Term, Term)>>` — insertion-ordered, unkeyed); kernel/src/context.rs:210-213 (`instances()` returns the raw slice); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1136-1153 (deferred instance obligations are resolved after the explicit arguments, and the solution is bound "directly (not via normalizing unification) so the instance stays structured"); kernel/src/context.rs:442 (`add_definition` — delta-transparent, and the only definition form: a `theorem` is just this with a `Prop` type); kernel/src/prelude.rs:923-1026 (`decEqBool` is registered exactly this way — a definition, then `add_instance` — the prelude's own worked example)
guards: Catches emitting ONLY the `add_instance` and not the `add_definition`. The instance would then resolve, but its value is an anonymous term with no global name, so it cannot be referred to, cannot be overridden, and appears nowhere in the certificate's dependency set — the certificate's `proof_term` would inline the whole dictionary.

Catches emitting ONLY the `add_definition`. Nothing scans definitions during resolution: `resolve_instance_at` iterates `ctx.instances()` and nothing else (elaborate.rs:1331-1340). A defined-but-unregistered instance is invisible, and since `class_heads` is also computed from `ctx.instances()` (elaborate.rs:1178-1189), the class itself becomes invisible too — a `[C α]` binder stops being treated as an instance premise at all. The error surfaces as `no typeclass instance found` (elaborate.rs:1147-1152) at a call site far from the omission.

Catches pushing the instance's BODY as the `value`. `add_instance(ty, body)` makes every resolution substitute the unfolded dictionary, so a program with n uses of one instance carries n copies of it. LOGOS's `Term` is a tree with no sharing (term.rs:443-545) and substitution is O(size) per binder (type_checker.rs:1088), so this is a quadratic blow-up, not just an aesthetic one. Push `Global(name)`.

Catches translating the instance's TYPE by its Lean name rather than by its elaborated form. The `ty` in `add_instance` is matched by UNIFICATION against the goal (elaborate.rs:1372-1375), so it must be the fully applied class type (`App(Global("Pointed"), Global("Nat"))`), not a `Global("instPointedNat")` and not a partially applied head.

Catches losing the anonymous instance's generated name. Lean names anonymous instances `instPointedNat`-style; LOGOS keys are flat `String`s (context.rs:449), so two anonymous instances of the same class at the same type — legal in Lean, and exercised by `dup₁`/`dup₂` below — generate the SAME name and the second `add_definition` silently replaces the first, while BOTH `add_instance` entries remain. The instance vector then contains two entries whose `Global` resolves to one body. See T02-020 and T07-008.
oracle: For each instance below: exactly one `add_definition` and exactly one `add_instance`, in that order; the `add_instance` value is a `Term::Global` naming that definition; the `add_instance` type is the fully-applied class type; and every emitted instance name is distinct.

cases.title: Simple instance resolution — a linear scan of a flat vector, run AFTER the explicit arguments
cases.lean: `[C α]` binder resolved by unification on a ground goal, method call at a known type
cases.target: A `ParamKind::Instance` binder whose metavariable is left as a deferred OBLIGATION during `elaborate_app_against`, then solved by `resolve_instance` once the explicit arguments (and the expected type) have pinned the class's type variables. The emitted term must be fully instantiated — no `?`-prefixed `Term::Var` may survive into the kernel.
evidence: kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1016-1027 (`ParamKind::Instance`: "resolved from the `Context`'s instance database — but only AFTER the explicit arguments have been processed, so any metavariable in the class type (e.g. the `A` in `Inhabited A`) is solved first"); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1044-1049 (`elaborate_app_against` — "The expected-type pass runs BEFORE instance resolution, so a class's type variable can be fixed by the context too"); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1136-1153 (the obligation loop; failure is `KernelError::CertificationError("no typeclass instance found for …")`); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1321-1341 (`resolve_instance_at`: `for (inst_ty, inst_val) in ctx.instances()` — a LINEAR SCAN in insertion order, each attempt on a CLONE of the metavariable context so failed trials never pollute it, first success wins); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1346-1400 (`try_instance` freshens the instance's parameter telescope to metavariables and unifies its CONCLUSION with the goal); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:138 (elaborator metavariables are `Term::Var` names beginning with `?` — never a `Term` variant, and they must be fully instantiated before the kernel sees the term)
guards: Catches emitting the instance argument as an unsolved metavariable. LOGOS's metavariables are `Term::Var("?0")` (elaborate.rs:138), which is a perfectly ordinary `Var` to the kernel — so `infer_type` reports `UnboundVariable("?0")` at best, and at worst the name collides with a binder and is CAPTURED by `substitute_avoiding` (type_checker.rs:1088), silently changing the term. Run `instantiate` and assert no `?`-prefixed variable remains.

Catches resolving the instance BEFORE the explicit arguments. The class's type variable is usually pinned only by an explicit argument (`Sized.size a` pins `α` from `a`'s type), so an eager resolver sees the goal `Sized ?0` and either fails or — much worse — matches the FIRST entry in the vector by unifying `?0` against that entry's carrier. `earlyResolution` below is the discriminating case: the first registered instance is at `Bool` and the call is at `Nat`.

Catches resolving from the EXPECTED TYPE only. `elaborate_app_against` runs the expected-type unification before instance resolution (elaborate.rs:1044-1049), which is how `Pointed.point` at an ascribed type resolves with no explicit argument at all. A translator that only ever pins from arguments fails `fromExpectedType` below.

Catches assuming resolution is CACHED or CANONICAL. It is neither: the scan runs afresh at every use site (elaborate.rs:1331) and is O(|instances|) each time, with a full `unify` per candidate. A development with hundreds of instances pays that on every method call, and because `try_instance` clones the whole `MetaCtx` per candidate (elaborate.rs:1332) the cost is in allocations, not just comparisons.

Catches treating a resolution FAILURE as recoverable. `elaborate_app_against` returns `Err(CertificationError("no typeclass instance found for …"))` (elaborate.rs:1147-1152); there is no backtracking into an alternative elaboration of the explicit arguments. A translator must therefore commit to one elaboration and report, not retry.

cases.title: Recursive / polymorphic instances — supported, and depth-bounded at 64
cases.lean: `instance {α} [C α] : C (F α)`, instance chains, recursion through a type constructor
cases.target: One `add_definition` + one `add_instance` whose `ty` is the instance's FULL type including its premises: `Π{α}. Sized α → Sized (Box α)`. `try_instance` peels that telescope, replaces each parameter with a fresh metavariable, classifies a parameter as a PREMISE iff its head `Global` is in `class_heads`, unifies the conclusion with the goal, and then resolves each premise RECURSIVELY at `depth + 1`.
evidence: kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1190-1198 (doc: "Handles POLYMORPHIC / RECURSIVE instances (`instance {A} [Inhabited A] : Inhabited (List A)`): the instance's parameter telescope is freshened to metavariables, its conclusion is unified against `required` (solving the type parameters), and each PREMISE parameter is then resolved RECURSIVELY. The first instance that fully resolves wins; failed trials never pollute `mctx` (each runs on a clone, committed only on success)"); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1346-1400 (`try_instance` — the telescope peel at :1360-1371, the premise test `head_global(&param_type).is_some_and(|h| heads.contains(h))` at :1365, the conclusion unification at :1373, the recursive resolve at :1380); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1158-1160 (`MAX_INSTANCE_DEPTH = 64` — "a backstop against a pathological instance set (`Inhabited A` from `Inhabited A`) looping forever"); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1327-1329 (the depth check `if depth > MAX_INSTANCE_DEPTH { return None }` — note it returns `None`, i.e. "no instance", NOT an error); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1174-1189 (`class_heads`, folded over registered instances' CONCLUSIONS)
guards: Catches registering the instance's CONCLUSION as its `ty` and dropping the premises. `add_instance(Sized (Box α), …)` with the `[Sized α]` premise elided would make `try_instance` see a conclusion with a free `Var("α")` and no telescope to freshen, so unification binds nothing and the instance either never matches or matches EVERYTHING. The whole premise mechanism lives in the `ty`'s `Pi` binders; there is nowhere else to put it.

Catches the ORDER dependency in `class_heads`. A parameter is classified as a premise only if its head is already in `class_heads` (elaborate.rs:1365), and `class_heads` is computed from the instances registered SO FAR (elaborate.rs:1178-1189). If a recursive instance is registered before any BASE instance of the same class, its `[C α]` parameter's head is not yet a known class head at the moment resolution runs — in practice `class_heads` is recomputed per call (elaborate.rs:1330) so the order of REGISTRATION is what matters, not of use. A translator must emit all of a class's instances before any consumer is elaborated, and must not interleave classes.

Catches the silent depth cutoff. At depth > 64 `resolve_instance_at` returns `None` (elaborate.rs:1327-1329), which is indistinguishable from "no such instance". The caller then reports `no typeclass instance found for …` (elaborate.rs:1147-1152) — a misleading message for a chain that DOES exist but is 65 links long. `deepChain` below is a 6-deep chain, well inside the bound; a translator that monomorphises a class hierarchy (T07-011's tempting escape) can easily exceed 64 and will then see this message with no indication that depth was the cause.

Catches assuming the premise's metavariable is solved by unification. It is not: `try_instance` binds it with `mctx.solve(name, resolved)` from the RECURSIVE call's result (elaborate.rs:1382-1387), deliberately keeping the nested instance structured. A translator that instead unifies the premise against the goal type loses the nesting and emits a flat dictionary.

Catches a premise whose head is NOT a class. `try_instance` treats any parameter whose head is not in `class_heads` as a type parameter to be solved by the conclusion unification (elaborate.rs:1364-1370). cases.title: `class ... extends` and the diamond it creates — LOGOS has no coherence checking
cases.lean: class extends, parent projections, a Foo/Bar/Baz/Qux diamond, `toParent` coercions
cases.target: Per derived class, ONE `add_structure` whose field list is the FLATTENED union of the parent fields and the new ones — because `add_structure` gives one projection DEFINITION per field and nothing else, there is no parent-as-subobject notion and no `toParent` to project. Then, per parent, a synthesised "forget" instance: `add_definition("Bar_toFoo", Π(α). Bar α → Foo α, λα b. Foo_mk α (Bar_op α b))` plus `add_instance(Π(α). Bar α → Foo α, Global("Bar_toFoo"))` so that a `[Foo α]` goal can be discharged from a `Bar α` in scope. Plus a loss record.

There is no `Term::Proj` (term.rs:443-545) and `add_structure` names projections `format!("{name}_{field}")` (context.rs:310-362, looked up by `elaborate_dot` at elaborate.rs:1284). `Global("Bar_toFoo")` resolves to nothing unless the translator explicitly emits it as a definition; a translator that assumes `add_structure` created it gets `UnboundVariable`.

Catches emitting the parent as a FIELD (`toFoo : Foo α`) instead of flattening. That is also a valid encoding, but it must be chosen CONSISTENTLY: mixing the two across a hierarchy means `Bar_op` exists on one class and must be reached as `Foo_op α (Bar_toFoo α b)` on another, and no call site can know which. Pick one and record it in the loss record.

Catches forgetting the forget-instances. Without `add_instance(Π(α). Bar α → Foo α, …)` a `[Foo α]` goal cannot be discharged from a `[Bar α]` binder at all, because resolution only ever looks in `ctx.instances()` (elaborate.rs:1331). Every Lean function that takes the PARENT class and is called with a CHILD instance breaks — which is most of a hierarchy's surface.

Catches forget-instances that shadow base instances. A forget-instance's conclusion is `Foo ?α` for a metavariable `?α`, which unifies with EVERY `Foo` goal. Inserted before the concrete `Foo Nat` instance, it captures all of them and then recursively demands a `Bar ?α` that may not exist — and the failure is reported as `no typeclass instance found for Foo Nat` (elaborate.rs:1147-1152), naming the wrong class. Forget-instances must be emitted AFTER every base instance.

Lean's `class Bar α extends Foo α` stores the parent as a single `toFoo` field (or flattens it, depending on `structureDiamondWarning` and on whether the parent is itself a flat structure), and `Bar.toFoo` is a real projection with a real coercion. The LOGOS encoding flattens, so the parent's *identity* is gone: after translation there is no term that IS the `Foo α` inside a `Bar α`, only a reconstruction `Foo_mk α (Bar_op α b)`. Two reconstructions from the same `b` are equal only by structure eta — which holds in `def_eq` (type_checker.rs:1391-1417) but NOT under `normalize`, so any proof that reaches the equality through `normalize` fails.

NO_COHERENCE. Lean warns (and Mathlib engineers around) the case where two paths through a diamond give different parent instances. LOGOS cannot even ask the question: `add_instance` appends to a vector (context.rs:184-186) and resolution returns at the first success (elaborate.rs:1334-1339). A diamond where `Qux → Bar → Foo` and `Qux → Baz → Foo` disagree is not detected, not warned about, and resolves to whichever path happens to be earlier in insertion order. The loss record must list every class reachable by more than one path so a human can check what LOGOS cannot. See T07-013 for the reject case.

ORDER_DEPENDENCE. Because resolution is insertion-ordered, the MEANING of a development depends on the order in which the translator emitted its instances. Translating the same Lean file with declarations visited in a different order can produce a different — still typechecking — LOGOS development. The loss record must pin the emission order so the result is reproducible.

cases.title: `outParam` / `semiOutParam` — no output-parameter concept; resolution unifies the WHOLE conclusion
cases.lean: outParam, semiOutParam, HAdd/HMul-style heterogeneous classes, Membership, GetElem
cases.target: (none — no sound translation)
evidence: kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1016-1027 (`ParamKind` has exactly three variants — `Explicit`, `Implicit`, `Instance` — with no per-ARGUMENT annotation of any kind on the class's own parameters); kernel/src/context.rs:71,184-186 (an instance is an unadorned `(Term, Term)` pair: there is no mask, no arity metadata, no output positions); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1346-1375 (`try_instance` unifies the instance's WHOLE conclusion against the goal — `if !unify(ctx, mctx, &conclusion, required) { return None }` at :1373 — so every argument of the class, output or not, must already be determined on the goal side or be solvable by that single unification); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1016-1027 again (`ParamKind::Instance`'s doc: resolution runs "only AFTER the explicit arguments have been processed, so any metavariable in the class type … is solved first" — the design assumes the class type is GROUND by then, which is precisely what `outParam` denies); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:138 (metavariables are `Term::Var` names beginning with `?` and must be fully instantiated before the kernel sees the term)
guards: THE TRAP: dropping the `outParam` wrapper and emitting the class as if all its arguments were ordinary. `outParam` is definitionally the identity (`outParam : Sort u → Sort u`), so erasing it produces a class that TYPECHECKS perfectly. What changes is resolution. In Lean, `HAdd α β γ` with `γ` an `outParam` means "resolve on `α` and `β`, and let the instance DETERMINE `γ`". With the wrapper erased, LOGOS's `try_instance` unifies the whole conclusion `HAdd Nat Nat ?γ` against each candidate — and `?γ` is a metavariable on the GOAL side, so unification will bind it to whatever the FIRST vector entry says (elaborate.rs:1331-1340, first-match-wins). The elaboration succeeds, silently, with the wrong output type; every later use of the result is then checked against a type the Lean source never mentioned. Because LOGOS is cumulative (type_checker.rs:1330-1360) the resulting terms very often still typecheck.

Catches the opposite failure — emitting `outParam` as a real global. It would then be an opaque `add_declaration` or a transparent `add_definition` wrapping the argument. Opaque: `HAdd α β (outParam γ)` never unifies with `HAdd Nat Nat Nat`, so no instance ever resolves and every arithmetic expression in the development fails. Transparent: `unify` normalizes it away and you are back to the first trap, having spent a global.

Catches "just require the output to be ascribed at every call site". That is not the same program. `a + b` in Lean elaborates with `γ` unknown; forcing an ascription changes elaboration ORDER, and LOGOS's expected-type pass runs BEFORE instance resolution (elaborate.rs:1044-1049), so the ascription would pin `γ` from the CONTEXT rather than from the instance — the reverse of what `outParam` specifies. Where the two disagree (a heterogeneous instance whose output is not the expected type), the translated program means something different.

Catches `semiOutParam`, which is subtler: it permits resolution to proceed with the position unknown but ALSO allows it to be used for matching. LOGOS has neither behaviour, and a translator that maps `semiOutParam` onto its `outParam` handling has conflated two different resolution orders.

Catches the scale error. `outParam` is not exotic: `HAdd`, `HSub`, `HMul`, `HDiv`, `HMod`, `HPow`, `HAppend`, `Membership`, `GetElem`, `Coe`, `MonadLift` and every `Bind`/`Functor` in Lean core use it. Rejecting it correctly rejects almost all notation-bearing Lean input — including the `+` in `n + 1`, unless the translator special-cases the homogeneous defaults, which is T07-007's problem.
oracle: Translator exits non-zero with E_NO_OUT_PARAM for every class below that has an `outParam` position, emits no `add_instance` for those classes, and in particular never emits an instance whose conclusion contains a `?`-prefixed `Term::Var`.
diag: E_NO_OUT_PARAM — must name the class, list the `outParam`/`semiOutParam` positions, and state that LOGOS resolution requires the whole conclusion to unify. Must NOT silently demote the `outParam` to an ordinary parameter.

cases.title: `@[default_instance]` — no fallback tier; LOGOS resolution either matches or fails
cases.lean: @[default_instance], instOfNatNat, instHAdd, numeric literal defaulting, `default_instance` priority tiers
cases.target: (none — no sound translation)
evidence: kernel/src/context.rs:71,184-186 (`instances: Arc<Vec<(Term, Term)>>` — a single flat list with no tier, no priority field, and no notion of "try this only if everything else failed"); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1321-1341 (`resolve_instance_at` — ONE linear pass over `ctx.instances()`; it returns at the first success and returns `None` if the pass completes with no match. There is no second pass, no fallback list, and no re-entry); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1136-1153 (an unresolved obligation is a hard `KernelError::CertificationError("no typeclass instance found for …")` — there is no "postpone and default later" path); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1044-1049 (`elaborate_app_against`: the expected-type unification runs BEFORE instance resolution, so by the time resolution runs the metavariables are either solved or permanently stuck); kernel/src/term.rs:13-44 and kernel/src/reduction.rs:330-345 (`Literal::Nat(BigInt)` is a KERNEL literal, definitionally `Succ^n Zero` via the `extract_constructor` bridge — LOGOS numerals do not go through a class at all, so there is no `OfNat` for a default instance to be the default OF)
guards: THE TRAP: translating `@[default_instance]` as an ordinary instance and relying on position. It is not equivalent in EITHER direction, and both directions break silently: • Emitted FIRST, the default instance captures every goal of its class, including goals a specific instance should have handled, because `try_instance` unifies its conclusion's metavariables against the goal (elaborate.rs:1373) and a default instance's conclusion is maximally general by design. Lean would have used the specific instance; LOGOS uses the default. The program still elaborates. • Emitted LAST, the default instance is only reached when nothing else matches — which looks right, but Lean's defaulting fires on a metavariable that is still UNSOLVED at the end of elaboration, whereas LOGOS's resolution runs at the point of the application with whatever is known then (elaborate.rs:1136-1140). A goal that Lean would default, LOGOS resolves eagerly against an earlier instance the moment enough of the type is known — or fails outright if it is not.

Catches the numeral-literal special case, which is where this bites hardest. `(2 : α)` in Lean is `@OfNat.ofNat α 2 inst`, and `instOfNatNat` is a `@[default_instance]` that makes a bare `2` a `Nat`. LOGOS has no `OfNat`: numerals are `Term::Lit(Literal::Nat(BigInt))` (term.rs:13-44), definitionally `Succ^n Zero` (reduction.rs:330-345, type_checker.rs:1480-1493). So every Lean numeral must be translated to a LOGOS `Nat` literal — and a numeral the Lean source intended as an `Int`, a `Float`, or a user type is then silently a `Nat`. `Int` in LOGOS is a completely different kind of thing: an OPAQUE type with axiomatised ring laws (prelude.rs:92-191), not an inductive, so `Nat` and `Int` literals are not interchangeable. See T10-004.

Catches `instHAdd`. Lean's `a + b` is `HAdd.hAdd` resolved through the `@[default_instance] instHAdd : HAdd α α α` fallback, which ALSO depends on `outParam` (T07-006). A translator that handles neither will see `+` as an unresolvable class method in essentially every Lean file; one that special-cases `+` to `Nat.add` has hard-coded a defaulting decision that the source did not make and that is wrong for every non-`Nat` carrier.

Catches emitting the default instance and ALSO the specific ones and calling the order a "policy". It is not a policy, it is a semantic change, and it must be reported. If a translator chooses to proceed anyway it has switched this case's verdict to `degrade` and owes a loss record naming the defaulted position and the instance it picked — but INDEX.md marks this `reject`, and this file follows that.
oracle: Translator exits non-zero with E_NO_DEFAULT_INSTANCE for every declaration below whose elaboration involves a `@[default_instance]`, and emits no `add_instance` for the defaulted class. A harness additionally checks that no emitted instance vector contains an entry whose conclusion is a bare `App(Global(C), Var("?…"))`.
diag: E_NO_DEFAULT_INSTANCE — must name the class and the defaulted metavariable, and state that LOGOS resolution has a single tier. Must NOT pick a default itself.

cases.title: Instance priority — LOGOS has none; resolution is first-match-wins in INSERTION order
cases.lean: `instance (priority := 900)`, `@[instance]` with priority, `attribute [-instance]`, `local instance`, Lean's later-declared-wins default
cases.target: A total ORDER on the emitted `add_instance` calls, chosen by the translator to reproduce Lean's resolution outcome, plus a loss record pinning that order. LOGOS offers exactly one lever: the sequence in which `add_instance` is called. Lean's default is "higher priority first, then LATER declaration first"; LOGOS's is "EARLIER insertion first". So the naive emission order — source order — inverts Lean's tie-breaking.
evidence: kernel/src/context.rs:71 (`instances: Arc<Vec<(Term, Term)>>` — a pair, with no priority field and no room for one); kernel/src/context.rs:184-186 (`add_instance` does `Arc::make_mut(&mut self.instances).push((ty, value))` — APPEND, no key, no sort, no dedup); kernel/src/context.rs:210-213 (`instances()` hands out the raw slice in insertion order); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1331-1340 (`for (inst_ty, inst_val) in ctx.instances() { … if let Some(result) = try_instance(…) { *mctx = trial; return Some(result); } }` — the scan returns at the FIRST candidate that fully resolves, and never looks at the rest); kernel/src/elaborate.rs:1190-1197 (doc: "The first instance that fully resolves wins; failed trials never pollute `mctx`")
guards: Catches emitting instances in source order and assuming it reproduces Lean. It inverts the default tie-break. `laterWins` below is the discriminating case: two equal-priority instances at the same type, where Lean picks the SECOND and a source-ordered emission makes LOGOS pick the FIRST. The translated program computes a different number and typechecks perfectly.

Catches sorting by priority and ignoring declaration order. Lean's rule is lexicographic — priority first, then declaration order (later first) — so a stable sort by descending priority over the SOURCE sequence still inverts every tie. The correct emission is: sort by descending priority, and within each priority band reverse the source order.

Catches assuming a more SPECIFIC instance wins. It does not: specificity plays no part in `resolve_instance_at`. A general instance `Show (Box α)` emitted before a specific `Show (Box Nat)` captures the specific goal, because `try_instance` freshens the general instance's `α` to a metavariable and unifies successfully (elaborate.rs:1360-1375). `generalBeatsSpecific` below is that case, and it is the one a translator is most likely to get wrong because Lean's behaviour here looks like specificity even though it is priority-plus-order.

Catches emitting a class's instances interleaved with another class's. Order matters only WITHIN a class in Lean, but the LOGOS vector is global and `class_heads` is recomputed from the whole vector on every resolution (elaborate.rs:1330,1178-1189). Interleaving makes the emission order harder to audit and makes any later edit to one class silently re-order another. Emit per class, contiguously, and record the blocks.
oracle: For every method call in this file, the instance LOGOS resolves is the one Lean resolves (checked by comparing the reduced values); the emission order is recorded in the loss record; the loss record names NO_PRIORITY and, for `localOnly`, NO_REMOVAL.
loss: NO_PRIORITY. Lean's priorities are a partial specification of resolution order that the author wrote down deliberately; LOGOS can only approximate them with a linear order. Where Lean's priorities are equal and it falls back to declaration order, the two systems disagree by DEFAULT: Lean prefers the later declaration, LOGOS the earlier. The translator must therefore emit instances of equal priority in REVERSE source order, and the loss record must say so — because the resulting LOGOS development no longer resembles the Lean source's declaration sequence, and a human reading it will draw the wrong conclusion about which instance wins.

NO_REMOVAL. `attribute [-instance] foo` and `local instance` have no counterpart: there is no API to remove or scope an entry once `add_instance` has pushed it (context.rs:184-186 is the only mutator). A Lean development that activates an instance in one section and deactivates it in the next cannot be expressed; the translator must either refuse the file or emit the union, and the union may resolve differently everywhere. `localOnly` below is the instance in question.

NO_DIAGNOSABILITY. Because resolution returns at the first success (elaborate.rs:1334-1339), LOGOS never discovers that a second instance would also have matched. There is no "ambiguous instance" report and no way to ask after the fact which instances were candidates. Everything a reviewer needs to check the translator's ordering decision must be in the loss record; it cannot be recovered from the LOGOS context.

cases.title: `DecidableEq` synthesis — only two decision procedures exist, and `deriving` is not a translatable construct
cases.lean: DecidableEq, deriving DecidableEq, instDecidableEqNat/Bool, structural DecidableEq for inductives and structures
cases.target: `DecidableEq α` ⟼ `Π(a:α). Π(b:α). App(Global("Decidable"), Eq α a b)` — there is no `DecidableEq` global; it is an abbreviation and must be expanded. `instDecidableEqNat`  ⟼ `Global("decEqNat")`  (prelude DEFINITION + `add_instance`) `instDecidableEqBool` ⟼ `Global("decEqBool")` (prelude DEFINITION + `add_instance`) For every OTHER type, the translator must translate the decision procedure that Lean's `deriving DecidableEq` handler GENERATED — an ordinary recursive function returning `isTrue`/`isFalse` — and then `add_definition` it and `add_instance` it. Plus a loss record: the generated procedure is not the Lean source.
evidence: kernel/src/prelude.rs:923-1026 (`register_dec_eq_bool` — "Decidable equality of `Bool` (`decEqBool : Π(a b:Bool). Decidable (Eq Bool a b)`) … registered as a `Decidable` INSTANCE, so `decide` can actually discharge `Eq Bool _ _` goals"); kernel/src/prelude.rs:1027-1194 (`register_dec_eq_nat` — `decEqNat`, by structural recursion on the first argument, with a nested `b`-match in the `Succ a'` branch at :1157); a grep of prelude.rs for `add_instance` shows these are the ONLY two decision procedures registered; kernel/src/prelude.rs:757-818 (`Decidable` itself, `Type 0`- valued with `isTrue`/`isFalse`); kernel/src/prelude.rs:820-922 (`of_decide_eq_true`, PROVEN not axiomatised — the bridge back to a `Prop`); kernel/src/termination.rs (the termination guard is a syntactic structural (Giménez) check; there is no well-founded recursion, no `termination_by`, no equation compiler — so a generated procedure must be structurally recursive to be accepted); kernel/src/type_checker.rs:254-260 (`Match` is POSITIONAL: `cases.len()` must equal the constructor count, in registration order; there are no patterns and no wildcards)
guards: Catches emitting `DecidableEq` as a class. It is an ABBREVIATION in Lean (`DecidableEq α := (a b : α) → Decidable (a = b)`), so there is no class to declare, no `DecidableEq_mk`, and no projection. A translator that emits it via `add_structure` creates a genuinely different type, and the resulting instances no longer unify with the `Decidable (Eq α a b)` goals that `decide` actually raises (prelude.rs:796-818).

Catches assuming an instance for `List`, `Option`, `Prod` or `String`. None of those types is in the LOGOS prelude at all (see T10-011/012/013/016), let alone a decision procedure for them. A translator must emit the type AND its procedure AND the instance, in that order, or escalate.

Catches translating the derived procedure's `match` without expanding it. Lean's generated code uses nested and wildcard patterns; LOGOS's `Match` is positional with exactly one case per constructor in REGISTRATION order (type_checker.rs:254-260). Getting the order wrong produces a procedure that typechecks and returns the wrong answer — `isTrue` where `isFalse` was meant — which then feeds `of_decide_eq_true` (prelude.rs:824-922) and yields a "proof" of a false equation. This is the soundness bug in this case and it is why the loss record is not optional.

Catches registering the emitted procedure as a DEFINITION only. Nothing scans definitions during resolution (elaborate.rs:1331); without the `add_instance` the procedure is unreachable and every `decide` on that type fails.
oracle: `natEq`/`boolEq` resolve to the prelude's `decEqNat`/`decEqBool` and are NOT re-emitted; `colourEq` and `pairEq` are accompanied by an emitted structurally- recursive procedure plus an `add_instance`, and a loss record naming DERIVED_CODE_IS_NOT_SOURCE; `intEq` and `listEq` are escalated. A harness checks every emitted `Match`'s case count against the inductive's constructor count.
loss: DERIVED_CODE_IS_NOT_SOURCE. `deriving DecidableEq` is a metaprogram (`Lean.Elab.Deriving.DecEq`) that runs in `MetaM` and cannot be replayed — see T09-006. What the translator can carry across is only its OUTPUT: the elaborated `Expr` of the generated instance. So the LOGOS development contains a decision procedure that appears in no Lean source file, whose correspondence to the Lean declaration rests on the derive handler having been correct. That must be recorded; it is not the same trust story as a hand-written instance.

NO_STRUCTURAL_SYNTHESIS_IN_LOGOS. LOGOS cannot synthesise a `DecidableEq` for anything. If the Lean source relied on Lean's synthesis and the generated term does not survive translation — because it uses nested patterns (T04-008), a wildcard (T04-010), `noConfusion`/`injection` (T03-018) or non-structural recursion (T04-018), all of which Lean's handler emits routinely — there is no fallback. The loss record must distinguish "translated the generated procedure" from "could not".

NO_DECIDABLE_FOR_INT. LOGOS's `Int` is OPAQUE with axiomatised order laws (prelude.rs:92-340); `le`/`lt` are `Int → Int → Bool` axioms (prelude.rs:352-515), not decision procedures, and no `Decidable (Eq Int a b)` instance is registered. A Lean `DecidableEq Int` therefore has NO target at all. `intEq` below is the case.

cases.title: `Inhabited` / `Nonempty` — neither is in the LOGOS prelude; both must be emitted
cases.lean: Inhabited, default, Inhabited.mk, Nonempty, Nonempty.intro, Nonempty.elim, `opaque` declarations' inhabitedness obligation
